strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper clearly identifies real methodological gaps in audio chaptering (transcript-centric evaluation, ASR dependence, lossy timestamp snapping), and the formalization of text-space (R1, H1-H3) and time-space (T1, T2) protocols is a genuine contribution that others in the area can adopt.

The protocol analysis is backed by concrete evidence: oracle experiments (Table A5) quantify the discretization ceiling (~73-81% F1), and Table A6 demonstrates that transcript granularity inflates text-space metrics while T1 preserves ranking, validating the proposed transcript-invariant evaluation.

The experimental scope is broad and well-designed around four explicit research questions: seven MiniSeg training/evaluation transcript combinations, six audio encoders for AudioSeg, hand-crafted feature ablations by category, and multiple MLLM strategies (zero-shot, chunking, ICL, self-cascaded, LoRA) with a detailed failure-mode analysis (Table A2).

The central finding that an audio-only model with a Whisper encoder outperforms all transcript-based models is interesting and well-supported, including a convincing control experiment (DeepFilterNet ablation showing F1 drops when non-speech audio is removed) and case analysis of non-speech cues at chapter transitions.

Reproducibility is strong: hyperparameters for all models, full prompts for LLMs, alignment and feature-extraction procedures, dataset annotations (duration regime, speaker regime, ASR variants), and a stated commitment to release code and annotations.
Honest and thorough limitations section acknowledging the single-dataset, English-only scope and computational constraints on fine-tuning larger MLLMs.
weaknesses: All conclusions rest on a single dataset (YTSeg). Given that the strongest result (AudioSeg > text models) may be partly driven by domain match of the Whisper encoder to YouTube data - which the authors themselves acknowledge - generalization of the headline claim is uncertain without even a small secondary evaluation or dataset.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting anywhere; differences of 1-3 F1 points (e.g., pause features +2.87, Ref+ASR_T vs. other MiniSeg variants) drive several conclusions, and some claims (e.g., ASR_T outperforming ASR_L despite worse WER) rest on small margins.

Protocol T2 (continuous-time, collar-based) is formalized and advertised as 'the most direct formulation' but is essentially unused in the experiments; the main evaluation uses only T1 with a single 6-second grid, and the paper does not analyze sensitivity of results to the chunk-size choice (even though delta_t is a free parameter that could interact with model behavior).

The protocol formalization is careful but the empirical comparison across protocols (Table A6) is limited to three MiniSeg variants; it would be stronger if applied to the audio-only and MLLM models, which is the main motivation for transcript-invariant evaluation.

The novel AudioSeg architecture is a fairly straightforward hierarchical adaptation of MiniSeg's design to audio frames; the architectural contribution is modest, and there is limited architectural ablation beyond swapping the frozen encoder.

MLLM conclusions are constrained (videos <30 min, only LoRA fine-tuning on the smaller Qwen2.5-Omni due to compute), so the claim that MLLMs 'remain limited' could reflect the specific models/prompts rather than the paradigm.

Some findings are under-explained, e.g., why models trained on ASR_L underperform ASR_T, and the interaction between training data duration distribution and the sharp performance drop beyond 20-30 minutes is only conjectured.

strengths: The formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1-H3, T1, T2) is a genuine and useful methodological contribution. The paper clearly articulates why transcript-dependent metrics are not transcript-invariant and why snapping continuous-time boundaries to sentence boundaries is lossy, and the oracle analysis (Table A5, F1 ceiling of 73-81%) provides concrete quantitative evidence for this claim rather than just asserting it.

The experimental scope is broad and well-organized around explicit research questions: three modeling paradigms (text-based, audio-only, MLLM), six audio encoders for AudioSeg, multiple ASR conditions, LoRA fine-tuning of MLLMs, and stratified analyses by duration and speaker regime. The failure-mode analysis of MLLMs (Table A2) is a nice touch that goes beyond headline numbers.

The paper is transparent about confounds, e.g., explicitly flagging that Whisper Large's advantage may stem from domain match with YouTube data, and honestly reporting where MLLMs fail (instruction following, generation loops, LoRA hallucinations) rather than burying negative results.

Reproducibility appears strong: hyperparameters for all trained models are provided (Tables A7-A9), prompts are included in full (Appendix B), feature extraction is precisely documented (Appendix F), and the authors commit to releasing code, AudioSeg, and their dataset annotations.
The writing is clear and well-structured; the distinction between text-space and time-space protocols is carefully motivated and easy to follow.
weaknesses: All conclusions rest on a single dataset (YTSeg), which is English-only and itself the source of the strongest result. The headline claim that transcript-free segmentation is 'superior' rests on Whisper Large - an encoder trained on data overlapping YTSeg's domain - which the authors themselves acknowledge. This makes the central claim difficult to generalize and somewhat circular; a single non-YouTube-domain evaluation would substantially strengthen it.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting for any comparison. Many of the reported differences are small (e.g., MiniSeg Ref+ASRT vs. MiniSeg ASRT+Features: 40.01 vs. 40.30 F1), and claims such as 'pause duration provides the largest gain' or the >=60-minute reversal (15.17 vs. 13.28 F1) are made without confidence intervals or multiple seeds.

The strongest empirical finding (pauses dominate acoustic gains) largely replicates what Freisinger et al. (2025) already observed, weakening the novelty of that contribution. The counterintuitive result that better ASR (Whisper Large) yields slightly worse segmentation than Whisper Tiny is left unexplained ('other factors are at play'), which is unsatisfying.

The proposed continuous-time protocol T2 is presented as the 'most direct formulation' of the task, yet the reported results are almost entirely computed under discrete T1; T2/collar-based evaluation is formalized but not used for the main comparisons, so the paper's own recommended protocol is under-exercised.

The AudioSeg architecture is a fairly straightforward adaptation of MiniSeg's hierarchical design to audio frames (frozen encoder + local transformer + RoFormer); its novelty is modest, and the 6-second chunk granularity is a fixed design choice whose sensitivity is not ablated, even though it directly determines task difficulty and metric behavior.

The MLLM conclusions are limited by context-length restrictions to <30-minute videos and by evaluating only two Qwen Omni models; given the rapid pace of the field, the generality of these findings is uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically relevant task (audio chaptering) with a clear diagnosis of its transcript-centric biases, and the proposed taxonomy of evaluation protocols (R1, H1–H3, T1, T2) is well motivated, clearly formalized, and arguably the paper's most durable contribution.

The transcript-invariance argument is convincing and empirically supported: the oracle analysis (Table A5, F1 ceiling of 73–81%) and the protocol comparison (Table A6) concretely demonstrate that text-space metrics can be inflated by transcript granularity rather than by better segmentation.

The experimental coverage is broad and systematic: multiple ASR quality regimes, multiple audio encoders (Whisper, HuBERT, AF3-Whisper, Qwen3-AuT, PEA-Frame), hand-crafted feature ablations, MLLM inference strategies (zero-shot, chunking, ICL, self-cascaded, LoRA), and stratified analyses by duration and speaker regime.

The findings are actionable and specific rather than generic: pauses drive most acoustic gains, speaker features matter only in multi-speaker content, ASR WER does not predict segmentation quality, and joint training on Ref+ASR improves robustness. The DeepFilterNet ablation (Table A1) is a nice causal check on the non-speech-cue hypothesis.

The paper is well organized and transparent: hyperparameters, prompts, alignment procedures, and feature extraction are documented in appendices, and the authors commit to releasing code, the AudioSeg model, and new dataset annotations.

The failure analysis of MLLMs (Table A2: missing transcripts, generation loops, WER, length ratios) goes beyond aggregate F1 and gives a fine-grained picture of why current MLLMs underperform on long audio.
weaknesses: All experiments are on a single English dataset (YTSeg). The authors acknowledge this, but it limits the generality of the central claims (e.g., 'transcript-free segmentation is superior'), and there is no held-out validation on any other corpus or domain.

The headline claim that audio-only modeling is superior is partially confounded: the best AudioSeg variant uses Whisper Large, an encoder trained jointly on transcripts and audio, so its advantage may stem from implicit ASR/linguistic knowledge rather than purely acoustic information. The paper notes this but does not resolve it; HuBERT's much weaker results (F1=35.58) are consistent with the confound rather than against it.

The main evaluation uses a fairly coarse 6-second discretization (T1). While this is justified by average sentence length, boundary placement errors up to ~6s are tolerated, and the continuous-time protocol T2 — presented as 'the most direct formulation of the task' — is formalized but not used for the main results, which weakens the paper's own argument for time-based evaluation.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported; several comparisons that carry interpretive weight (e.g., +2.87 F1 from pauses, ASR_T vs ASR_L differences, MLLM T vs T+A gaps of a few points) are small relative to typical dataset variance.

There is a potential fairness asymmetry: AudioSeg is trained and evaluated natively on the 6s time grid, while text-based models and MLLMs must be mapped to the grid via forced alignment of (possibly predicted) transcripts, adding an error source that AudioSeg avoids. This is disclosed but not ablated.

MLLM results are restricted to videos <30 minutes and LoRA fine-tuning is applied only to Qwen2.5-Omni (the weaker of the two models), so the 'MLLMs are promising on shorter audio' claim rests on a narrow slice of the evidence.

Reproducibility currently depends on promised releases: no code, annotations, or model checkpoints are verifiable at review time, and some details (e.g., exact LOESS smoothing in Figures 2–3, chunk-grid label assignment for boundary timestamps) are underspecified.

The comparison space stops at text/audio; no baselines from adjacent tasks (e.g., topic segmentation or video chaptering methods adapted to this setting) are included, which makes it harder to gauge absolute progress on the task.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated methodological gap: audio chaptering has been treated as a text-segmentation problem on transcripts, and the paper clearly articulates why this framing conflates transcript quality/granularity with segmentation quality.

The formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) is precise and useful. The distinction between text-space and transcript-invariant time-space protocols, plus the oracle analysis (Table A7) quantifying the inherent lossiness of transcript-based projection, is a solid methodological contribution that will benefit future work.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: three modeling paradigms (text-based with/without acoustic features, a new audio-only architecture, MLLMs), two ASR quality regimes, six audio encoders, multiple prompting strategies for MLLMs, duration/speaker stratification, and out-of-domain validation on AMI.

Several interesting and non-obvious findings, well-supported by ablations: pause duration dominates acoustic gains; speaker features help specifically in multi-speaker regimes despite small overall gains; ASR WER correlates only weakly with segmentation performance; MLLMs can localize topical boundaries but fail at precise temporal grounding (evidenced by the FA vs. predicted-timestamp gap in Table 7).
The DeepFilterNet ablation (Table A1) is a nice causal validation of the non-speech-cue hypothesis.
Strong reproducibility: hyperparameters, prompts, feature extraction details, failure-mode analysis, and public release of the evaluation toolkit, AudioSeg, and released annotations.
weaknesses: Findings rest primarily on a single dataset (YTSeg), English-only; the AMI validation is very small (16 val/test meetings), so cross-domain and multilingual generalization claims remain weakly supported.

No statistical significance testing or seed variance is reported anywhere; given the moderate effect sizes in several tables (e.g., pause features +2.87 F1, speaker features +0.67 F1), some conclusions rest on differences that could plausibly be within run-to-run noise.

Potential confound in the headline claim that AudioSeg 'substantially outperforms' text-based models: the best audio encoder is Whisper Large, an ASR encoder trained on YouTube-like data, and AudioSeg is evaluated natively at its 6s resolution while text-based models are mapped via forced alignment to the same grid. The authors acknowledge the domain-match possibility, but the comparison could be confounded by resolution/discipline alignment; a controlled analysis (e.g., AudioSeg evaluated after re-binning only, or text models evaluated at finer alignment) would strengthen the claim.

The AudioSeg architecture is a straightforward composition of known components (frozen audio encoder, local transformer windowing, RoFormer document encoder); the novelty lies in the system-level result rather than architectural innovation.

Protocol T1's chunk size (6s) is chosen to match average sentence length, which is reasonable, but the observed non-monotonic re-discretization artifacts (Table A8) and reliance on default Pk parameters indicate the protocol analysis, while careful, is not fully airtight.

Minor presentation issues: several typos and reference formatting errors (e.g., 'Barrére', 'Watzel', Zechner venue), Figure 3 axis reversal (1.0 to 0.4) is unconventional, and the title-quality analysis (Section 5.3/Table A11) is comparatively thin relative to its prominence in the contributions.
The claim that 'transcript-free segmentation is not only viable but superior' is stated too strongly given the domain-match caveat and single-dataset evidence.

strengths: The formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2) is a genuine methodological contribution: it makes explicit the domain mismatch between continuous-time chapter boundaries and discrete transcript units, and the oracle analysis (Table A7) convincingly quantifies the inherent ceiling (~73-81% F1) of transcript-space evaluation, providing principled motivation for time-based, transcript-invariant evaluation.

The empirical study is broad and well-structured around explicit research questions: transcript quality (Q1), acoustic feature contributions with per-category ablations (Q2), MLLM capabilities including temporal grounding and title quality (Q3), stratified analyses by duration and speaker regime (Q4), and protocol reliability (Q5). The analysis goes beyond aggregate metrics (e.g., non-speech cue filtering via DeepFilterNet validating the music/sound-effect hypothesis; FA vs. predicted-timestamp comparison isolating temporal grounding as the MLLM bottleneck).

AudioSeg is a reasonable and clearly described audio-only baseline showing that transcript-free segmentation can outperform text-based models (F1=45.52 vs. 40.30), with a useful encoder comparison across six pre-trained audio encoders and an honest discussion of why ASR-pretrained encoders dominate.

Reproducibility support is strong: hyperparameters for all models (Appendix D), full prompts (Appendix C), feature extraction details (Appendix G), released toolkit and augmented YTSeg annotations (duration regimes, speaker regimes, ASR transcript variants), and failure-mode statistics for MLLMs (Table A2).
The paper is clearly written, includes an honest limitations section, and the cross-domain check on AMI, while small, supports the main conclusions.
weaknesses: Reliance on a single primary dataset (YTSeg), which is English-only and originates from the same research lineage as the MiniSeg baseline; the AMI validation uses very few test meetings (4 in the <30min subset), so the cross-domain evidence is weak and generalizability claims rest essentially on one benchmark.

No statistical significance testing or multi-seed variance reporting anywhere in the paper. Several headline claims rest on small margins (e.g., MiniSeg + Features 40.30 vs. +Pauses 40.17 vs. Ref+ASR_T 40.01 on F1), so the conclusion that 'pause duration drives nearly all gains' could be noise; the granularity analysis in Table A8 even shows non-monotonic AudioSeg behavior (45.52 vs. 42.01 at 8s), which is acknowledged but undermines confidence in precise orderings.

The architectural novelty of AudioSeg is modest: a frozen encoder, a small local transformer with [SEG] pooling, and a RoFormer boundary classifier with BCE loss is a fairly standard composition; the main insight (Whisper encoder features carry chaptering-relevant structure) is empirical rather than a methodological advance, and the paper does not probe why Whisper Large works (e.g., probing, layer analysis) beyond a plausible domain-match conjecture.

A potential confound is not fully controlled: Whisper Large was pretrained on YouTube-scale data that likely overlaps the YTSeg distribution, which could inflate the audio-only result relative to text-based models trained only on YTSeg transcripts; the DeepFilterNet ablation partially addresses acoustic-cue usage but not this pretraining-overlap concern.

MLLM experiments are restricted to <30 minute videos and primarily one model family (Qwen Omni), with LoRA fine-tuning only on the smaller Qwen2.5-Omni (acknowledged as compute-limited); claims about MLLM limitations are therefore based on a narrow slice of the model landscape.

The choice of 6s chunks is justified by average sentence length, but Pk and Boundary Similarity were designed for sentence-level sequences and their behavior on 1s-resolution time grids is not validated; the reliance on default segeval parameters for time chunks (Appendix F.1) is a methodological detail that deserves more justification.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper correctly identifies that audio chaptering has been treated as a purely textual task and that standard text-space evaluation protocols are not transcript-invariant. The formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1–H3, T1, T2) in Section 2 is a genuine methodological contribution that will be useful beyond this paper.

The central empirical finding is well supported: AudioSeg (audio-only, F1=45.52) substantially outperforms the best text-based baselines (~40), and the DeepFilterNet ablation (Table A1) plus qualitative analysis of non-speech cues (music, sound effects) gives a plausible mechanism rather than just an aggregate number.

Broad and well-organized experimental design organized around explicit research questions (Q1–Q5), covering transcript quality robustness, individual acoustic feature ablations (pauses dominate at +2.87 F1), encoder comparisons, duration/speaker stratification, and out-of-domain validation on AMI with transfer results.

The MLLM analysis is insightful: disentangling segmentation ability from temporal grounding via the predicted-timestamp vs. forced-alignment comparison (F1 12.52 vs. 43.84) is a clean diagnostic, and the failure-mode analysis (Table A2) is thorough.
The oracle analysis (Table A7, ceiling F1≈73–81% under sentence-boundary projection) convincingly quantifies the lossiness of text-space protocols and motivates time-based evaluation.
Good reproducibility posture: hyperparameters (Tables A12–A14), full prompts (Appendix C), feature extraction details (Appendix G), released toolkit and model, publicly released dataset annotations.
Honest limitations section acknowledging single-dataset (YTSeg) reliance, English-only scope, and computational constraints on fine-tuning larger MLLMs.
weaknesses: No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported anywhere. Several headline claims rest on differences of 1–3 F1 points (e.g., MiniSeg feature ablations in Table 5, ASR quality results in Table 4), which may not be robust given a dataset of this size.

The strongest claim — 'transcript-free segmentation is not only viable but superior' — has a potential confound: the best AudioSeg uses Whisper Large, whose pretraining data is similar in domain to YTSeg, and the authors themselves note 'possibly aided by domain match'. The architecture is also fairly simple (windowed frozen features + RoFormer), so novelty is modest, and it is unclear how much of the gain is encoder choice vs. architecture vs. training data coverage.
Validation on the second dataset (AMI) is very small (16 test meetings), so the out-of-domain conclusions have limited statistical power; the paper is effectively a single-benchmark study.

Primary evaluation uses a 6s discretized grid chosen to match average sentence length, which arguably re-introduces a discretization choice of the kind the paper criticizes; the authors mitigate this with multiple chunk sizes (Table A8) and T2 collar-based scoring, but the non-monotonicity at 8s/10s chunks and its explanation are somewhat hand-wavy.
MLLM conclusions are restricted to videos <30 minutes due to context limits, so the MLLM portion of the comparison is not fully commensurate with the other paradigms on the full dataset.

The title quality evaluation (Appendix B) is reasonable but excludes unmatched chapters under TM, which could bias comparisons toward models with more (possibly spurious) boundaries; no human evaluation of chapter coherence or title quality is provided.

Some claims would benefit from more careful support: the statement that ASR quality 'does not directly translate to segmentation performance' is based on Whisper Tiny vs. Large comparisons with a single training configuration, and the mechanism for why ASR_L-trained models underperform is left speculative.

Relevance to ACL is real but the paper straddles speech/NLP; a strict reading of scope might see the MLLM and evaluation-protocol contributions as the core NLP-relevant parts, with the acoustic modeling being more ICASSP-flavored.
